title: SRE Documentation: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review Standards, Operational Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This page consolidates Redwood Inference SRE guidance for defining and operating Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. The intent is to provide a single, operationally actionable reference for oncall SREs, service owners, and platform engineers.

Scope

- Applies to production-facing inference services (Redwood API, routing/edge layer, model-serving runtime, and platform control plane).
- Not a replacement for product-specific playbooks; links to service-level runbooks are provided in the Appendix.

Executive summary

- Define measurable SLOs with clear owner and measurement window.
- Error budgets are the primary enforcement mechanism for releases and capacity policy changes.
- Capacity planning uses rolling forecasts and headroom targets tied to error-budget burn rates and business growth signals.
- Post-incident reviews follow a blameless, timeline-driven template with remediation and reliability initiatives tracked quarterly.
- A lightweight operational tooling stack (dashboards, automated alerts, runbook playbooks) is mandatory for all high-risk services.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

1.1 SLO Principles

- SLOs must be: customer-centric, measurable, and owned by a product or platform team.
- Use a small set (typically 2-4) of SLOs per logical service: Availability (error-rate), Latency (p50/p95/p99), and optionally Quality (model-level correctness / hallucination rate) for important workloads.
- Measurement window: default rolling 30d for operational decision-making, 90d for strategic trends.

1.2 Recommended SLO targets (defaults for hosted Redwood API)

| Metric | Target | Measurement window | Alerting trigger (>=) | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| API availability (5xx errors and 4xx customer errors normalized) | 99.95% | 30d rolling | 99.90% | api-platform-team |
| Request latency (p95 end-to-end, user request->first-token) | <= 500ms | 30d rolling | p95 > 700ms | runtime-serving-team |
| Request latency (p99 end-to-end) | <= 1200ms | 30d rolling | p99 > 1500ms | runtime-serving-team |
| Model response correctness (evaluations / synthetic prompts) | >= 98% for selected cohorts | 30d rolling | 96% | applied-ml-team |

Notes: Targets are adjustable per service and customer tier (e.g., Dedicated customers may have stricter targets). Document service-specific SLOs on their runbook pages.

1.3 Error budget policy

- Error budget = 1 - SLO. Burn is calculated daily on a rolling 30d window.
- Action thresholds: 
  - Green: burn rate <= 1x expected - normal operations.
  - Yellow (action required): rolling 7d burn rate >= 2x expected or remaining budget <= 30% - require review and temporary soft freeze on risky changes (no non-critical releases).
  - Red (mitigation required): remaining budget <= 10% or 7d burn rate >= 5x expected - rollback risky changes, enable mitigations, convene rapid reliability review.
- Error budget ownership: service owner is responsible for coordinating mitigation; SRE will recommend mitigations (capacity, routing, feature toggles).

1.4 Release gating and feature rollout

- No major release that increases risk to SLOs is allowed while the service is in Red.
- Canary windows should be sized to consume at most 5% of error budget in steady state.
- Progressive rollouts must include automatic rollback criteria tied to SLO signals (p95 latency, error-rate).

2) Capacity planning and operational headroom

2.1 Forecasting cadence

- Inputs: historical QPS, token throughput, customer committed capacity (Dedicated), marketing/product events, model changes (new larger models), regional load shifts.
- Cadence: weekly short-term (1-4w) forecasts maintained by SRE; monthly medium-term (1-3m) reviewed with product; quarterly strategic (3-12m) capacity commitments for Dedicated contracts.

2.2 Headroom targets and scaling policies

- Headroom goal: maintain at least 30% spare steady-state capacity in Hosted clusters for critical services; Dedicated and Private customers can have custom headroom per contract.
- Autoscaling signals: CPU/GPU utilization, queue length, tail latency (p99), and scheduling backpressure metrics.
- Burst capacity: configured to allow 1.5x baseline for short duration (<= 10 minutes) before invoking throttles or degradation policies.

2.3 Capacity runbook snippet (daily checks)

- Check cluster GPU utilization > 85% on sustained 10m window -> create paging alert.
- Check scheduling queue length increase > 3x baseline -> open incident if accompanied by latency impact.
- Verify healthy capacity for top 20 tenants (Dedicated) and top 50 API keys (Hosted) in the last 24h.

3) Reliability initiatives and investment process

3.1 Initiative lifecycle

- Triage: post-incident problems or trend analysis produce candidate initiatives.
- Prioritization: use RICE-like scoring with additional reliability ROI dimension (expected error-budget savings + cost savings).
- Delivery: timeboxed projects (4-12w) owned by a cross-functional team (SRE, Runtime, Applied ML).
- Measurement: define KPI (error-budget burn reduction, latency p95 improvement, cost per token).

3.2 Example initiatives (past 12 months)

- KV cache prefix compression - reduced median token-cpu by 18%, improved p99 latency during steady load.
- Smart routing by model variant - reduced P95 latency for low-cost routes by 25% and saved ~$120k/month.
- Automated model fallback on GPU OOM - eliminated 40% of capacity-related incidents.

4) Incident review standards and postmortems

4.1 Incident severity classification

- Sev 1 (P0): Platform-wide outage or major impact to all customers (>1h degraded availability or critical SLA breach).
- Sev 2 (P1): Significant degradation affecting many customers or a major customer with measurable business impact.
- Sev 3 (P2): Localized or transient issues with minor business impact.

4.2 Postmortem requirements (for Sev1/Sev2; recommended for Sev3)

- Timeline (what happened, in chronological bullet points).
- Impact summary (customers affected, duration, SLO burn, financial impact estimate if available).
- Root cause analysis (multiple hypotheses evaluated; final RCA and evidence).
- Corrective actions (short-term mitigations and long-term remediation).
- Action owner for each corrective item, and due date.
- Learnings and metrics to track progress.

4.3 Postmortem review process

- Draft within 72 hours; completion within 10 working days for Sev1/Sev2.
- Blameless review led by SRE with product and engineering stakeholders; meeting scheduled within 7 days of incident close.
- Track remediation items in the Reliability Initiative backlog; quarterly review of outstanding items.

5) Operational tooling and observability standards

5.1 Required dashboards and metrics

- Per-service SLO dashboard (availability, p50/p95/p99 latency, request volume, error budget burn).
- Capacity dashboard (cluster utilization, per-GPU metrics, queue length, scheduling rejects).
- Impact dashboard for top customers (latency, success-rate, request volume).

5.2 Alerting guidance

- Alerts must be actionable and tied to a runbook. For each alert, define: symptom, likely causes, runbook link, severity, and paging policy.
- Alert tiers:
  - Pager (immediate action): SLO breach, sustained cluster CPU/GPU > 90%, scheduling queue > threshold with latency impact.
  - Email / ticket: anomalies without immediate service degradation (minor increases in error rate).
  - Self-heal automation: trigger autoscaling or routing changes where safe.

5.3 Runbook automation and playbooks

- Keep short, reproducible CLI commands and console links in runbooks. Include commands for toggling fallbacks, adjusting routing weights, and increasing capacity.
- Where possible, automate safe mitigations (e.g., scale-up jobs, remove noisy tenant from shared capacity) and ensure a human-reviewed rollback path.

6) Canonical SRE runbooks (examples)

Note: Each runbook below must be linked from the service-specific Confluence page and kept under source control.

6.1 Runbook: High p95 latency for Hosted API

- Symptom: p95 latency exceeds threshold for > 5 minutes and p99 trend increasing.
- Initial checks (5 minutes):
  1. Check SLO dashboard (region, route, model variant).
  2. Inspect scheduling queue length and per-GPU utilization for the serving pool.
  3. Identify recent deploys or config changes in the last 30 minutes.
  4. Verify model size changes or quantization profile changes in rollout.
- Immediate mitigations (ordered):
  1. Add capacity to affected pool (scale up nodes or increase instance count); verify circuits.
  2. Enable degraded-mode routing: shift non-critical traffic to lower-cost, low-latency variants or cached responses.
  3. Increase batching timeout carefully (only if throughput-driven).
  4. If correlated with a release, perform targeted rollback.
- Post-incident: run full postmortem, estimate SLO burn, and propose a reliability initiative if root cause is systemic.

6.2 Runbook: GPU capacity exhaustion / OOMs

- Symptom: scheduler rejects increase, GPU OOMs logged, or abrupt drop in throughput.
- Initial checks:
  1. Confirm OOM logs and node-level GPU memory usage.
  2. Identify tenants with sudden spikes (top talkers).
  3. Verify recent model uploads and quantization configuration changes.
- Immediate mitigations:
  1. Temporarily scale up with pre-warmed nodes or burst capacity.
  2. Evict or throttle noisy tenants per policy; notify customer success for Dedicated customers.
  3. Enable model fallback to smaller-parameter variant.
- Longer-term actions: improve admission control, add graceful degradation for memory-heavy requests, and add automatic early rejection for requests that will OOM.

6.3 Runbook: KV cache corruption or cache inconsistency

- Symptom: cache hit rate drops suddenly or cache miss pattern correlated with higher latency and cost.
- Immediate checks:
  1. Validate cache health metrics and replication lag.
  2. Check recent schema/config changes to cache keys or TTL.
- Mitigations:
  1. Roll back key schema changes or TTL config.
  2. Prime cache from warm snapshots if available.
  3. Temporarily disable cache-dependent routing and accept higher token-cost routing until stability restored.

7) Ownership, escalation, and change management

- Ownership: SRE owns platform-level SLO definitions and alerts; product / service owners own customer-facing SLOs and runbooks.
- Escalation path: runbook -> service owner -> oncall tech lead -> SRE manager -> exec incident lead. Contact matrix must be kept updated in each runbook.
- Change management: any change to SLO targets, alert thresholds, or runbook playbooks requires a change record and review by the Reliability Working Group (bi-weekly).

8) Templates and artifacts (appendix)

8.1 Postmortem template (paste into new page)

- Title: Postmortem - [Service] - [Short description] - [DATE]
- Severity: Sev1|Sev2|Sev3
- Timeline: bullet list with timestamps (UTC)
- Impact summary: customers affected, SLO burn, user-facing behavior
- Root cause: succinct statement + evidence
- Corrective actions: list with owner and due date
- Preventative actions / reliability initiatives: list with owner and success criteria
- Review notes: meeting date, attendees

8.2 Standard alert table (example)

| Alert name | Symptom | Severity | Runbook | Pager? | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| api-p95-high | p95 > 700ms (30m) | P1 | /runbooks/high-p95 | yes | runtime-serving-team |
| cluster-gpu-oom | GPU OOM rate > 5/min | P0 | /runbooks/gpu-oom | yes | infra-gpu-team |
| routing-5xx-increase | 5xx rate > baseline + 0.5% | P1 | /runbooks/5xx-rate | yes | api-platform-team |

8.3 SLO & Alert configuration (example JSON snippet)

- Please store production SLO definitions in the central SLO repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/slo-defs. Each service must include: slo_id, metric_source, measurement_window, target, owner, alert_thresholds.
